Stronger PI model (Gemini 3.1 Pro) diagnoses, Gemini 3.5 Flash implements. Complete MLE-Bench: 70.7% medals at 24h (ties prior best), 76.0% at 48h; competitive on PostTrainBench; per-task research notes. Self-reported; belief updates deliberately simple.

entries.title: Why caching model outputs doesn't pay off
entries.by: Sean Goedecke, seangoedecke.com, 2026-11-20
entries.summary: Output tokens cost more than input, and agents repeat code and evidence back, so teaching models to emit references the harness expands looks attractive. But in his agent histories only about 6% of output is visible text (50% reasoning, 44% tool calls), so even cutting two-thirds of it saves about 4% (Amdahl). Real savings come from smarter models needing fewer reasoning tokens and tool calls (pricier per token, cheaper per task); providers likely already exploit repeats via n-gram speculative decoding. Anecdotal split; measure your own.

entries.title: RL post-training in diffusion transformers is mostly a constant steering shift
entries.by: Meral, Oktay, Helbling, Kara, Chau and Yanardag (Virginia Tech, Georgia Tech), arXiv 2611.26627; shared by Tuna Meral
entries.summary: One fixed set of steering vectors added to a frozen base model's block outputs, the same for every prompt, token and seed (0.29M params vs an 18.8M RL LoRA on SD3.5-M), fitted to match public RL-tuned checkpoints with no reward, recovers 90.0-96.3% of six image models' reward gains and 89.8%/111.9% on two video models; trained directly with online RL it beats weight-based RL on OCR and PickScore. Reading: RL mostly steers toward what the model could already do. Useful as a cheap baseline and a reward-hacking check; diffusion only.

entries.title: Spec-driven development gaps: rules that drift, expensive search, and lost intent
entries.by: Oscar Benedek (IBM), oscarbenedek.com, November 2026
entries.summary: An internal SDD framework for IBM Bob beyond Spec Kit/OpenSpec: stacked org/repo/folder RULES.md (higher wins); lifecycle hooks re-inject rules and run checks after tool use and at stop (the main gain); a condensed "yellow pages" index with a navigation skill and a prompt-submit reminder to use it before grep/glob (cost -17 to -45%, tool calls -33 to -58% on 3-7 self-run questions; no correctness measure); cross-repo context via a dependency map and GitHub Enterprise MCP; plans compacted into change history after review.

entries.title: RAG chunk size is the last knob: measure, fix boundaries, restore context
entries.by: Hao Hoang, LinkedIn, 2026-11-21 (interview-question series)
entries.summary: Loosely relevant results come from chunks that lost their subject (too small) or mix topics (too large), so changing size only swaps failures. Order: a labelled retrieval eval with recall@k first; structure-aware splitting with 10-20% overlap; contextual notes prepended before embedding (one model call per chunk); match small, send the parent section; tune size last against the eval. Practitioner advice, no new data.

entries.title: Train LLM From Scratch: every post-training objective on one hand-written Transformer
entries.by: FareedKhan-dev/train-llm-from-scratch (Fareed Khan, MIT); shared by Mayank A.
entries.summary: A plain-PyTorch Transformer (no trl, peft or transformers) carried through pretraining, SFT with assistant-only loss masks, a Bradley-Terry reward model, DPO/ORPO/KTO/IPO/SimPO, PPO with a value head and GAE, and GRPO with Dr. GRPO, DAPO and GSPO flags, all on one backbone via a single forward_hidden method. A --arch modern flag swaps in RoPE, RMSNorm, SwiGLU, GQA/MLA, MoE and a KV cache; Muon, LoRA, speculative decoding and int8 are hand-written too. A 369K-param TinyStories model trains on a laptop CPU in about 5 minutes. Strongest evidence: its base eval matches lm-evaluation-harness on GPT-2 to 0.0006 per log-likelihood. Weakest: reward model and DPO both at 0.574 accuracy and no published GSM8K numbers for post-training stages, so the RL stages teach mechanics, not gains. Widest objective coverage of the three from-scratch repos (R097, R120).

entries.title: Deferred scheduling for agent runs: off-peak model capacity in Google ADK
entries.by: Google ADK docs (Python 2.10.0); shared by Shubham Saboo
entries.summary: `RunConfig(service_tier=DEFERRED)` queues every model call in a run for discounted off-peak Gemini capacity (tiers: deferred, flex, standard, priority); the tier is per run, so one agent serves live and batch traffic. ADK polls the queued interaction for you. Sharp edges: each tool-using turn queues separately (latency multiplies by turn count); no client deadline by default; a timeout or disconnect stops polling but the backend still runs and bills; unsupported models silently fall back to standard with one log warning; no streaming.

entries.title: Stretch evals: a practitioner's Gemini 4 Neon result on incident-investigation tasks
entries.by: Shahram Anver (Cleric), LinkedIn, 2026-11-20
entries.summary: Cleric keeps a "stretch" tier of eval cases its incident-investigation agent fails today and makes it harder as models catch up. On it Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.2 Sol both score 78.8% recall (Sol about 1.5x faster and 30% cheaper); Gemini 4 Neon scores 98.1%, but is too slow and costly without its in-memory cache, which the team is tuning. A production shadow run is next. Caveats: set built from incumbent failures (selection bias favours any new model), size and run counts not given, recall only, uncached numbers. Practices: keep a stretch tier beside the main suite, promote cases once they pass, compare at equal harness and caching, gate model switches on a shadow run.

entries.title: LeanRDF: untrusted search finds, a proven checker certifies knowledge-graph reasoning
entries.by: Volland/rdf-lean (Apache-2.0); shared by André Lindenberg
entries.summary: Lean 4 libraries encoding W3C RDF 1.2, RDFS, OWL 2 RL/EL, SPARQL 1.1 and SHACL Core semantics. Elpi (or a SQLite SPARQL store) searches and emits certificates; a checker proven sound turns accepted ones into theorems, so search bugs can only cause rejections. SPARQL and SHACL engines proven exact; no sorry, no extra axioms; W3C suites largely pass (SHACL 98/98, RDFC 86/86). Sound not complete ("not derived" is not "false"); thousands of triples, not millions; early single-maintainer repo.

entries.title: OpenComputer: a steerable cloud coding agent that lives in the Slack thread
entries.by: diggerhq/opencomputer (Apache-2.0); shared by André Lindenberg
entries.summary: An open-source cloud coding agent that runs in a Slack thread: one outbound-only VM per install, one Claude Code, Codex or OpenCode session per thread under rootless Podman, and teammates can steer it mid-task (messages land after the current tool call); results arrive as PRs. The vendor's latency benchmark on a trivial dependency bump shows low overhead but says nothing about hard tasks. Risks: prompt injection via the thread, secrets in the shared view, path-dependent runs.

entries.title: AlphaProof Nexus settles a 2017 photonics question with a Lean-checked no-go proof
entries.by: Krenn, Firsching, Tsoukalas, Gajjala, Gu and Chaudhuri (Tübingen, Google DeepMind); shared by DAIR.AI
entries.summary: AlphaProof Nexus (frontier LLMs plus Lean compiler feedback) found a proof that no linear-optics setup with photon-pair sources can produce high-dimensional GHZ states for even N ≥ 4 and D ≥ N, settling a 2017 question; humans then gave it a physical reading. The trust boundary is the formal statement: a faithful encoding makes it as solid as Lean's kernel, a subtly off one makes a correct proof of the wrong claim.

entries.title: AutoRAGBench: coding agents build RAG systems from scratch and beat published designs
entries.by: Zhang, Pan, Zhong et al. (Tsinghua, Sina Weibo); shared by Elvis Saravia
entries.summary: Coding agents get six hours and one H800 to build a RAG system from scratch on nine tasks, with the test set outside the container, an audit gate before scoring and five answering models grading retrieval. The best agent (GPT-6.1 Sol with Codex CLI) averaged 56.1 against 44.4 for the best published method per task, but every agent-built system retrieved 1.4 to 5.8x slower, and a quarter submitted a version worse than their own peak.

entries.title: Git Ontology Agent: steering a running agent with request branches and typed claims
entries.by: gogoymh/git-ontology-agent (MIT); shared by Minhyeong Yu
entries.summary: A same-day prototype that keeps agent work state as typed claims with dependencies in a git repo, one branch per user request. A decision model classifies each mid-task message as supplement, correction, independent, cancel or progress; only dependent claims are redone, and branches merge claim by claim with per-type rules. Answers are worded from claim status and replayable from commits. Open gaps: who writes the dependency edges, and side effects already taken.

entries.title: Zed Delta: review the agent thread, not the pull request
entries.by: Zed Industries; shared by Sam Keen
entries.summary: Zed's Delta (public beta) makes the agent conversation thread the unit of collaboration and review instead of the pull request. Teammates join a thread, ask the same agent why it chose something, and review in subthreads with isolated worktree copies whose fixes fold back before landing. DeltaDB records edits between commits beside the messages that caused them, while staying Git-compatible. Tradeoffs: longer narratives to read, lock-in of the narrative, and review gates to re-express without PRs.

entries.title: Claude Code Code Mode: the agent writes a script instead of calling tools one at a time
entries.by: Claude Code documentation; shared by Addy Osmani
entries.summary: An experimental Claude Code mode where the model writes a short JavaScript program, run through a REPL tool, that makes many tool calls itself: in parallel, chained, and filtered so only what matters reaches context. Per-call deny/ask rules and PreToolUse hooks still apply, but the auto-mode classifier sees the program, not runtime values, so hard limits belong in rules, hooks or a sandbox. The JavaScript and its file, web and MCP calls run outside the shell sandbox.

entries.title: G-MTP: a built-in multi-token drafter speeds Gemma 4 decoding up to 3.1x
entries.by: Galgani, Ji, Homburger, Jawahar et al. (Google); shared by DAIR.AI
entries.summary: A multi-token-prediction drafting head built into Gemma 4: one shared head reads the target's own activations, cross-attends to the target's KV cache with zero copy (no second prefill or cache), and scores clustered vocabulary instead of a full softmax. Reported speedups up to 3.1x on large models, 2.3x for small models on H100 and 2.2x on a phone GPU; recipes keep the drafter aligned after domain fine-tuning. Gains depend on acceptance rate, batch size and sampling settings.

entries.title: Pointable work: how long an agent can run alone depends on who could fool its check
entries.by: André Lindenberg, Artificial Engineering newsletter
entries.summary: A job is pointable when the instruction names an existing thing that judges the result, and an agent can run alone only as long as its check holds. A ladder of checks, each harder to fool: the agent's own word, tests it can edit, a recorded original it cannot edit, and a small formal statement with an untouchable checker. Five conditions for unattended work: an authority, a recordable boundary, a check the agent cannot edit, shipping half done behind a fallback, and something looking outside the check.

entries.title: fast-anything: port only the hot functions to Rust, gated on replayed real calls
entries.by: EL4CTEO/fast-anything (MIT); shared by André Lindenberg
entries.summary: A tool that profiles a running app, ranks pure functions by time spent times portability, records up to 500 real calls, and has a coding agent port only the hot ones to Rust. Each port must replay every recorded call plus derived edge cases (NaN, empty, non-ASCII, 16x larger) answered by the original, and be faster per call, before it swaps in behind a reversible switch. Author's runs show 3x to 116x on fuzzy dedupe; only deterministic plain-data functions qualify.

entries.title: LangChain 101: measured answers on harness choice, durability and structured output
entries.by: AI Engineering from Scratch (rohitg00/ai-engineering-from-scratch); shared by Dr. Alvaro Cintas
entries.summary: A free, roughly 390-page manual on LangChain 1.5, LangGraph 1.2, Deep Agents 0.7 and LangSmith where every listing comes from a recorded run. Its measured answers: a plain tool loop, create_agent and a hand-built StateGraph gave identical outcomes on 60 of 60 tasks; create_agent costs about 5 ms a call; Deep Agents used 3.6x to 4.3x the prompt tokens; a node re-ran after a crash in 97 of 100 trials under every durability mode; structured-output strategies failed outright on a small local model.

entries.title: LogT: better tool-use data beats heavier RL for visual search
entries.by: Fu, You, Guo, Lu, Akula, Wu, Liu, Dutta and Yuan (credited to Meta Superintelligence Labs and UMD); shared by Brenn Hill, resharing Javier Medel
entries.summary: LogT (NeurIPS 2026) argues the bottleneck for VLMs that zoom into images is poor fine-tuning traces, not RL. An automated engine writes questions about small objects in SA-1B images, filters them with a separate judge, and builds traces following three strategies: answer directly, multi-hop via an anchor, or exhaustive regional search. A 7B model fine-tuned on these beats prior SFT+RL methods on seven benchmarks with 3.1x less data and over 120x fewer GPU hours; part of the gain is distillation from 72B and 106B teachers.

entries.title: Accept agent code on evidence, not line-by-line review
entries.by: Paul Iusztin; Matt Pocock on The Pragmatic Engineer
entries.summary: Two practitioners converge: Paul Iusztin says reading every line of agent code is mostly wasted effort and acceptance should rest on criteria, tests, static, type and security checks, and realistic runs; Matt Pocock says TDD's ritual matters less for agents but the evidence matters more, asking for a test that fails without the change and passes with it, and warns of tautological tests. The reviewer's job shifts to auditing evidence, with line review triggered by risk, novelty or a failed check.

entries.title: EfficientSkill: learn the skill for accuracy, then prune it for tokens
entries.by: Shah, Badhe, Kathrotia and Tiwari (credited to Google and Purdue); shared by DAIR.AI
entries.summary: Reflective skill optimizers bloat skill files with edge-case rules. EfficientSkill first repairs a minimal seed skill for accuracy with no token penalty, then prunes it under an accuracy floor by compressing rules, bounding turns into compact workflows, and offloading reusable code into workspace utilities. Against unconstrained EvoSkill across four models and three benchmarks, output tokens fell in 11 of 12 configurations (up to 80%) and mean accuracy rose on every benchmark. Pruning straight from the seed stalls.

entries.title: Managed Agents and Clief's folder workflow, explained
entries.by: Jake Van Clief (reel) and Anthropic Engineering
entries.summary: Jake Van Clief's reel claims Managed Agents makes custom harnesses a waste of time and vindicates building on files and process. Anthropic's design splits brain (Claude plus a stateless harness), hands (lazily provisioned sandboxes and tools) and an append-only session log, cutting p50 time to first token about 60%. Clief's ICM folder workflow (a one-screen map, routing rows, staged folders, scripts) maps cleanly onto mounted repos, memory stores, outcomes and permission stops. Verdict: own your folder, rent your runtime; harness work moved, it did not die.

entries.title: mobile-agent-testers: one AI tester per phone configuration, in CI
entries.by: pierridotite/mobile-agent-testers (MIT); shared by André Lindenberg
entries.summary: A GitHub Actions template that builds a mobile app once, then fans out one Claude Code exploratory tester per phone persona (device, OS, font scale, dark mode, locale, RTL), each filing bug reports with numbered screenshots and an accessibility probe. On LocalSend, 20 phones found 46 distinct bugs in 69 minutes for $4.62, most on a single configuration. It finds new problems rather than giving deterministic pass/fail, so triage and scripted regressions are still needed.

entries.title: BuggyMLE: harder coding evals by injecting verified bugs into working ML repos
entries.by: Wu, Qiang, Zhuang et al. (Google Research, Google DeepMind, UIUC); shared by Elvis Saravia
entries.summary: A Code Complexity Index of ten structural features (repo size, dependencies, files, hunks and lines changed) predicts average solve rates across eight coding benchmarks with R² ≈ 0.95. BuggyMLE uses that as a dial: an agent injects verified bugs into working ML repos to a mutation budget, an oracle isolates which ones matter, and a solver is graded on recovered metrics. The best of 14 models falls from 95% to 9% across tiers; silent bugs that leave validation intact are fixed far less often; a 9B model trained on the curriculum rivals frontier models.

entries.title: Anthropic's Forward Deployed Engineer path: 9.5 hours, and the 100 minutes that make it FDE
entries.by: Hao Hoang
entries.summary: Anthropic's Forward Deployed Engineer path on its partner academy: 11 self-paced courses, about 9.5 hours. Nine are shared with the Claude Developer path; the two FDE-specific courses (100 minutes) cover delivery, not code: qualify the use case, agree success measures and capture a baseline before building, ship a first slice, then drive adoption. Seven courses are in the public Academy. Gaps: no eval, security, cost or post-pilot operations course, and it prepares for the Foundations exam rather than Professional.

entries.title: Jetriever: rank every agent memory by usefulness, not similarity
entries.by: Li, Zhang, Du and Mao; shared by Zelal Gungordu
entries.summary: Jetriever skips the similarity shortlist: a small LLM-derived decision model scores every stored memory for the probability it helps answer the query. On InMind's 125 indirect queries it ranks the gold memory first 84.8% of the time (BM25 1.6%, MiniLM 0%) and reaches 76% end-to-end application against at most 16% for published systems, near the 84% oracle. A general 9B model recognises as many gold memories in its top 50 but only 40% at rank 1: calibration, not recognition, is the hard part. Cost grows linearly with the pool.

entries.title: Cross-model PR review: fan out, verify disagreements, don't vote
entries.by: Adhish Thite
entries.summary: One read-only orchestrator sent the same diff, CI results, comments and repo rules for a 150-file PR to Claude, Codex and Gemini, each splitting the work across its own sub-agents. Verdicts split. A separate synthesizer checked every disagreement and solo high-severity claim against the code instead of voting: it dropped 2 false positives and kept single-model catches, leaving 41 verified findings with agreement scores, handed to a separate fix run. Open issues: the synthesizer shares a family with one reviewer, no human spot check, differing severity scales, no cost given.

entries.title: Four frontier-lab papers, mid-November 2026: vision in agent work, world-model flips, test-time adaptation, small-model RL
entries.by: Tom Anusic (roundup of four arXiv papers)
entries.summary: Four mid-November papers that each find a gap existing measurements hide. MKA: 200 professional tasks that need vision; removing image viewing leaves GDPval unchanged but costs about 6 points here, and no model clears 57%. Flip Test: 11 video world models score at best 18.3% on counterfactual frame pairs, below random. Test-time adaptation: in-context replay lifts a 9B agent from 28.8% to 49.4%, GRPO on top reaches 51.6% and restores skipped verification. LoCoJAX: host orchestration is 36% of a small-model GRPO step on TPU; local rollouts run 1.3-3.6x faster.

entries.title: Warp's self-improving agents: feedback becomes a reviewed skill edit
entries.by: Michael Segner (claude.com), shared by Claude for Business
entries.summary: Each Warp agent (PR review, issue triage, spec writing) runs a base skill. A scheduled improver skill pulls human feedback from PR and issue comments, compares the agent's output with how people reacted, and opens a PR with the smallest edit to the base skill; a human reviews and merges. Advice: principles not rules, explain why, capture feedback where work happens, keep skills small, don't conflate skills with memory, assume feedback is sometimes wrong. Gaps: no before/after quality numbers, no replay or regression check before merge, no pruning.

entries.title: GrepMem: keep summarising, but let the agent grep the verbatim log
entries.by: Yang, Shi and Zhao (USC); shared by Pascal Biese
entries.summary: Keep summarising to hold working memory small, but first append every message and tool output verbatim to a plain-text log, and give the agent a regex search tool over it. With an RL-trained 9B model, exact recall far past the context window reaches 95-97% against at most 21% for summarisation or observation masking, and it beats summarisation by 8.8 points on multi-question research sessions. No embeddings, index or extra model. Limits: one model, controlled benchmarks, and the agent needs a keyword to search for.

entries.title: Outbox plus inbox under chaos: four ways to wire one sale to one message, measured
entries.by: Lukas Grigis
entries.summary: Four ways to wire one sale to one message, measured under seeded chaos (kill -9 on apps and broker, Toxiproxy dropping confirms and acks) and counted from both databases. Save-then-send lost 274 of 1,316 committed sales; send-in-transaction made 25 ghosts; a Spring Modulith outbox lost none but applied 25 twice; outbox plus a Postgres inbox (INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING in the consumer's transaction, settle after commit) gave zero of each. Gotcha: since RabbitMQ 4.3 released deliveries skip the quorum-queue delivery limit. One machine, one run per variant.

entries.title: Microsoft's 12 Nov 365 outage: a four-month-old defect, a quiet failover and missing headroom
entries.by: Microsoft preliminary post-incident report via The Register; summary by Suresh G.
entries.summary: A July gateway fix caused lock contention that only bit on many-core hardware under peak load. Teams failed over onto Exchange's gateway while 14% of capacity was already out; retry-to-next-healthy cascaded to over 80% of servers unresponsive in about two hours, restored servers were re-flooded, and rollback was impossible for four-month-old code, so engineers shipped a revert-to-known-good patch in waves. Lessons: load-test on production-class hardware, treat failover as a change, compute in-service headroom, admit traffic gradually on recovery.
